## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Fleet operations briefs

One file per UTC day, `YYYY-MM-DD.md`: what the fleet actually accomplished that day,
and one project worth returning to. Written each morning by the `fleet-digest` task in
this repo's own local pack.

**The dated series is the point.** A brief exists for every day the fleet has been
running, including the days nothing happened — a quiet day says so in one line. That is
what makes a *missing* file legible as a fault rather than as a slow Tuesday.

## How a day becomes a brief

1. **Prework** (code, 05:00 UTC) enumerates every active member, collects the pull
   requests merged and issues closed during the previous UTC day, drops the Claudinite
   maintenance PRs that land in every member nightly, ranks what is left **by size of
   change**, and keeps a shortlist half again longer than the brief needs.
2. **The agent** reads only that shortlist and picks the strongest few — new projects
   first, then biggest improvements, then most complex work — at 20 words apiece. Size
   gets an item onto the shortlist; judgment gets it into the brief.

The task ends there, at a landed file. On a day with nothing to rank, step 2 is skipped
entirely and prework writes the brief itself — there is no judgment in "nothing
happened", and no reason to pay a model for it.

## Backfilling

To catch up after an outage, or to seed the series when it starts: run the
**Claudinite scheduler** workflow manually with

```
overrides: FORCE_TASKS=fleet-digest,DIGEST_BACKFILL_DAYS=7
```

It covers the N most recent complete UTC days, oldest first, and **skips any day that
already has a brief** — so it is safe to re-run and safe to overlap with the daily task.
Quiet days land directly; the rest go to one agent dispatch that writes them all in a
single PR. Bounded at 30 days a run.

Backfilled briefs are written *as-of the morning after their own day*, so a Tuesday from
last week gets the brief that Tuesday would have got — its own accomplishments, and
whatever was quiet **then** — rather than last Tuesday's work with today's neglect
stapled on.

## Getting it read

An ad-hoc session later in the day, whose own notification mechanism does the delivering.
Its whole instruction:

> Read `digests/<yesterday's UTC date>.md` and send it as a notification verbatim.
> Nothing else: no other files, no tests, no commands, no edits.

The second line is the load-bearing one. Left to its own devices a session will read the
repo to "understand" the brief, and what arrives is a re-summary of a summary.

**That is why a brief is plain text despite its `.md` name.** The notification renderer
parses no markdown and collapses every line break, so a brief written in markdown reaches
the owner as its own source code in one running paragraph. Each item opens with `• ` — a
separator that survives the collapse — and carries its URL bare, which the renderer
autolinks. The `digest-plain-text` check holds the landed series to it. This file is
documentation *about* the series, is read on GitHub, and is markdown on purpose.

## Configuration

On this repo's `sheepdog` pack entry in `.claudinite-checks.json`, under `digest`. Both
keys default; an absent block still writes the file.

| key | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `pick` | `4` | how many accomplishments the brief names (the shortlist is `ceil(pick × 1.5)`) |
| `nudge` | on, 7 days | the "worth returning to" prod. `false` switches it off; `{ "quietDays": 21 }` widens the window |

**Quiet is measured on meaningful merges, never on pushes.** Every member's mount is
converged nightly, so `pushed_at` is fresh on every repo in this fleet every day and
would report the whole fleet as permanently active.

## Secrets

`FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` — the account-spanning PAT the other fleet sweeps already read
with. The digest uses its **Pull requests: read** on top of what the census asks for.
Nothing else: the task writes a file and stops.

World sweep green locally.

1. **`.claudinite/local/packs/sheepdog-local/`** — the machinery that *writes* the digests: the `fleet-digest` task (`task.md`, `task.mjs`, `worker.mjs`, `collect-fleet-day.mjs` + tests) and five checks (`digest-plain-text`, `digest-config`, `dated-fixture-collision`, `fleet-exclude-shape`, `managed-workflow-drift`). ~2,500 lines, no reference to the old repo name anywhere in it — it is portable as-is. Already migrated before this PR: `preferences/` (both files, pointer repointed).

# Sheepdog — this repo's own rules

What this repo has learned about being the fleet **enforcer**. The canon under `.claudinite/shared/` is
mounted and read-only; lessons land here.

## The session that designed a task must not be the one that runs its judgment

A task whose agent stage exercises judgment — pick the strongest, rank these, decide what
matters — has to run that stage in a context that never saw the task being built. The
session that just spent hours choosing the ranking heuristic knows which candidates it had
in mind when it chose, and will find them again. That is not judgment, it is an echo.

So when a design session wants to exercise the thing it just built, the run belongs in a
subagent whose context starts empty, or in the scheduler where it was always going to
happen. Never inline in the design session.

The stronger form is to make the clean context structural rather than remembered: state it
in the task file itself, as a rule the agent reads every time. `fleet-digest`'s task.md
does — *"Do not load context you were not given... the candidate's own title, body and
discussion are what you have, and they are enough"* — which means the production path is
already clean without anyone having to arrange it. A discipline that depends on the
operator remembering is one that holds until the first busy night.

## Load a deferred MCP tool by its full `mcp__github__…` name

`ToolSearch`'s `select:` form matches the **registered** tool name, so `select:issue_read` finds nothing
and costs a second search before the run can read its own dispatch issue. Ask for
`select:mcp__github__issue_read` (and the same prefix for every other one) the first time.

The prompts that send you there name tools informally — `resolve-dispatch.mjs`'s `needs-issue` exit says
"the issue-get tool", which is not any tool's name. Translate to the `mcp__github__` name rather than
typing the phrase you were handed.

## `Grep` needs `output_mode: "content"` — `-n`/`-A`/`-B` on their own are silently ignored

The harness `Grep` defaults to `files_with_matches`, so a call carrying context flags but no
`output_mode` answers *"Found 1 file"* and none of the lines it asked for. Nothing errors, which is
why it keeps happening: **11 of the 58** `Grep` calls in this repo's whole log corpus were shaped
that way, across nine sessions from 2026-07-31 to 2026-08-16. Every one but the single call that
genuinely matched nothing cost at least one more tool call — four re-issued the same pattern with
`output_mode` added, two dropped to `Bash grep -n`, and #218 gave up after two tries and `Read` a
mounted module end to end for the two lines it wanted. A twelfth call that same night reached for
ripgrep's `-l` and was rejected outright (`unexpected parameter -l`); the tool spells that
`output_mode: "files_with_matches"`, which is already the default.

Ship the whole shape the first time:

```
Grep { "pattern": "…", "path": "…", "output_mode": "content", "-n": true, "-C": 3 }
```

## A canon skill lives under its pack — there is no `.claudinite/shared/skills/`

Read it at `.claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. The flat path is the
natural guess and it does not exist, so the guess costs a failed `Read` and a search before
the skill is even open. Three separate sessions on 2026-08-09 each spent that round-trip on a
different skill (`prose-to-checks`, `single-branch-status`, `generate-project-instructions`) —
it is not one agent's slip, it is what the layout invites.

You usually do not have to guess at all: whatever sent you to the skill — a task file, another
skill — linked it by relative path. Follow the link you were given instead of reconstructing
the path from the skill's name.

**With one exception, and it is the common one on a scheduled run: a link inside a `SKILL.md` you
loaded with the `Skill` tool.** That tool announces *"Base directory for this skill:
`/home/user/Sheepdog/.claude/skills/<name>`"*, and that directory holds **`SKILL.md` and nothing
else** — it is a flat mirror, not the pack. So every relative link the skill writes for its real
home (`../../extracting-lessons.md`, `../<sibling>/SKILL.md`) dangles from the base dir it just
gave you. On 2026-08-14 the growth-extract run read the link it was handed at
`.claude/skills/extracting-lessons.md`, got *"File does not exist"*, and paid a `find` to recover
`.claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/extracting-lessons.md`. Resolve a loaded skill's
own links against `.claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/` — the canon path — never
against the announced base directory.

## A fallback `ScheduleWakeup` needs a `prompt`, and a rejected one leaves you with no fallback

Waiting on a dispatched subagent, the executor arms a fallback wakeup in case the completion
notification never lands. `ScheduleWakeup` rejects `{ delaySeconds, noop, reason }` with
"`prompt` is required when `stop` is not true" — `reason` is not the wake instruction. Arm it
with the call the accepted runs used:

```
ScheduleWakeup { "delaySeconds": 1200, "noop": true,
                 "reason": "fallback while the subagent runs; its notification is the primary wake",
                 "prompt": "<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>" }
```

and `ScheduleWakeup { "stop": true }` to cancel it once the subagent reports.

**Ship the call, because describing the argument has measurably not worked.** This rule landed
2026-08-09 (#109) saying to "pass `prompt`", in prose. Every executor run since that armed a
fallback — #138 (08-11), #162 (08-12), #176 (08-13), #188 (08-14) — emitted the identical
rejected shape `{ delaySeconds, noop: true, reason }`, and **none of the four re-issued**: one
wakeup call apiece, all rejected. The three runs that were accepted (#153, #157, #177) all passed
`prompt` with that same `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` sentinel. A rule that names an argument is
the same defect as a rule that names a script without its command line (below) — the agent is
composing the call, not reading prose about it.

The failure is worth a rule because of what follows it, not because of the typo: on both nights it
happened the error scrolled past mid-turn, nothing retried, and the executor went on to say it would wait
for the notification — believing it held a safety net it had never armed. A 45-minute subagent whose
notification is lost then hangs the run to its own timeout. So when a call whose whole purpose is a
fallback is rejected, re-issue it before continuing; an unarmed backstop is the one error that stays
invisible until the thing it was guarding actually fails.

## When this repo reads the fleet, filter the machinery out of *every* stream it reads

Anything here that ranks fleet activity — what merged, what closed, what a member has been up
to — is reading a fleet whose busiest actor is Claudinite itself. Exclude the machine's own
artifacts on **each** axis you collect, not just the first one you thought of. A guard written
for pull requests while issues go through unfiltered leaves the whole hole open (`isMaintenance`
did exactly that, #117).

The reason this bites harder than ordinary noise: rank by size or by discussion and the
machine's own bookkeeping does not merely appear in the results, **it wins them.** A dispatch
issue collects a comment per executor stage, so it out-weighs the work it dispatched — three of
one day's six shortlist slots were `[claudinite-task]` issues. The brief then reports the
scheduler back to the owner as the owner's own accomplishment.

appears under an explicit `node --test`. A pack that ships checks should have its own tests run by
something that runs every cycle, or its breakage waits for whoever happens to look.

## A rule that names a canon mechanism expires with it — an empty dedup grep is the warning

On 2026-08-13 this file gained a rule saying a member's `claudinite.updated` can be held
*backwards* by `heldStamp()` while the repo converges normally, so freshness must be judged by
`ref`. **It was already false when it was written.** At that same HEAD the vendored mount said so
outright — `packs/basics/tasks/baselining/worker.mjs:88`, *"The stamp is no longer HELD for a
pending note (#768 Phase 4)"* — and #168's newest comment had retracted the explanation the rule
was built on. A day later the whole `baselining` task was gone from the mount entirely.

The run did grep `heldStamp` across `.claudinite/shared/packs/` and got one unrelated hit. It read
that emptiness as *"no canon rule covers this, so the lesson is new."* An empty dedup grep has a
second reading, and it is the likelier one when the candidate rule names a mechanism: **the thing
you are about to write down no longer exists.** So when a rule names a canon identifier — a
function, a field's semantics — grep the identifier in the mount's *code* and read the hit before
landing it. No hit means expired, not novel.

Two habits that would also have caught it: read an issue's comments to the **last** one (a
correction can itself be corrected — #168 has three, and the third retracts the second), and
remember that concurrent scheduled runs read the same issues minutes apart, so what is "newest"
moves underneath you mid-run.

That rewrite closed on a survivor — *"judge a member against canon head by `ref`"* — and the
survivor expired inside a day. See the next rule; do not restate canon's freshness measure here at
all.

**An absence is a mechanism too, and it expires fastest.** On 2026-08-16 this file gained
*"`queue/instructions.md` is a stale pointer — canon has never vendored it"*, and it was honestly
earned: a `find` and a `grep` over the whole mount that day returned no file, only the two
`invoke.mjs` comments promising one. It told the next queue-dispatched session to skip the file its
own routine prompt named. The very next converge (`bfc43e1`, 2026-08-17) vendored 79 lines of
exactly the procedure the rule said did not exist, so twenty hours after landing the rule was advice
to ignore the mount's own instructions — the shortest-lived entry this file has had. The mount
converges here **nightly**: a claim about what canon does *not* carry has a shelf-life of one night,
where a claim about a mechanism canon *does* carry at least decays at the speed of a redesign. So
report a gap on an issue, where a converge can close it (#226 and #228 both carry that one), and
keep this file for what a session should **do**.

The `ref` survivor above was derived exactly as the rule prescribes, by grepping the mount's
**code**: `packs/sheepdog/tasks/fleet-roster/drift-issues.mjs` classifies a member by the age of its
stamped ref and says so in its own header. At that same HEAD, the same pack's `RULES.md` said
the opposite — *"the update flows stamp `engineVersion` and `packVersions` and deliberately never
write `ref` or `updated`, so on a maintained member the stamped ref is FROZEN and its age
measures nothing"* — and neither identifier appears anywhere in that pack's code:

```
grep -rn "packVersions\|engineVersion" .claudinite/shared/packs/sheepdog/
```

returns the one `RULES.md` line and no module. The prose states a design the vendored code has not
implemented; the two landed in consecutive mount updates (#180, #181), so a session reading either
half alone comes away certain and wrong.

So the code grep is a **necessary check, not a settlement**. When a canon claim decides something
here, read both the pack's `RULES.md` and the module the task actually executes, and expect them to
disagree while a design is mid-landing — the module is what runs, the `RULES.md` is where canon
states intent. And restate neither: a local rule that copies canon's current measure is a copy on
canon's clock, which has now gone stale twice in three days on this one question. Name the artifact
that decides and send the reader there.

One paragraph of `engine/scheduler/executor.md` §4, two adjacent instructions, five consecutive
executor runs (#177, #176, #173, #182, #184):

- Names a file — *"check it against that ceiling with `verify-outcome.mjs`"*: **0 of 5** ran it
  first try.
- Ships a command — *"record the execution in code — one command:"* over a fenced
  `node … record-exec.mjs …`: **5 of 5** ran it first try.

All five probed the first: `--help` (which prints nothing), then `ls`/`cat`/`Read` of the source,
then a hand-built `node -e` import — two to four tool calls, at the end of a run, every night.

This file has carried *"`verify-outcome.mjs` has no CLI — import it"*, with the working one-liner,
since 2026-08-11 (#142). It took in **none** of the five. A corrective rule filed in a different
file does not repair a defective instruction — the agent is reading the instruction, not the
correction. (Contrast the deferred-MCP-name rule above: it fires while the agent is *at* the step
it governs, and 4 of these 5 runs got the `mcp__github__` prefix right first try.)

So in anything this repo writes that tells an agent to run something — its own task files, its
worker prose, an issue that hands work on — ship the **literal invocation** in a fenced block, not
the file's name. And when a landed lesson keeps not taking, check whether it is filed somewhere its
reader never opens before writing it down a second time.

## Look a `Claudinite tracker:` issue up with `in:title` **and** a narrow `fields` list

Every recurring task here opens by finding its tracker by exact title, and two 2026-08-12 runs each
paid for a different half of that one call. The growth-extract run searched the bare title:
`search_issues` matches **semantically**, so the ranked results led with this task's own
`[claudinite-task]` dispatch issues and the tracker needed a second, reworded query. The tidy-issues
run anchored correctly with `in:title` — canon's `git-github-advanced` skill says to — but left
`fields` unset, so two full-body responses overflowed the inline limit, were persisted to files, and
cost four `python3` slicing calls to read two issue numbers back out.

Pass both. `mcp__github__search_issues` with `"<exact title>" in:title` and
`fields: ["number","title","state"]` returns the tracker in one compact call.

## A background `Agent` dispatch shares this checkout — the parent's Stop hook can misread its WIP as its own

#204 dispatched a `core/update` apply-stage fix to a background `Agent` and correctly ended its
own turn once the dispatch was placed. The parent's Stop hook then fired **two blocking
findings** (`stop-hook-git-check.sh`: uncommitted changes; `task-lifecycle`: no commit
references an issue) — neither of which was the parent's own state. A background `Agent` runs
in the *same* working directory rather than an isolated worktree, so the subagent's in-progress
`git mv` staging was sitting in the shared tree and the parent's own hook read it as a violation
it had caused. The parent spent ~8 tool calls (`git status`, reading unrelated files,
`ListAgents`) reacting to a finding it could not fix — the commit belonged to the subagent —
before confirming via `ListAgents` that the subagent was still live and going back to waiting.

When a Stop-hook git/task-lifecycle finding fires while a background `Agent` is active on this
checkout, check `ListAgents` **first** rather than diagnosing the diff as your own: an
in-progress subagent sharing this tree is a live, ordinary explanation for uncommitted or
unreferenced changes that are not yours to fix, and the right response is to keep waiting for
its own completion, not to stage or commit on its behalf.

## The ask

`fleet-digest` — the task that writes the fleet's daily operations brief — lives as a **local** pack in the fleet enforcer repo (`missingbulb/Sheepdog`, `.claudinite/local/packs/sheepdog-local/`). It is generic fleet machinery with nothing repo-specific in it, and it should be a sixth task of the canon `sheepdog` pack alongside `fleet-roster`, `fleet-add-missing-packs`, `fleet-usage`, `fleet-pack-seeds` and `fleet-baseline`.

## Why now

`missingbulb/Shepherd` is replacing Sheepdog as the fleet enforcer. The digest **series** has already been carried over (missingbulb/Shepherd#23 — 15 briefs, 2026-08-02 … 2026-08-16, history that cannot be regenerated because a brief is written as-of the morning after its own day). The machinery that writes it has not, and re-landing it as a second repo's local pack would be a copy of a mechanic from a sibling repo — the tell that it belongs centrally. So the choice is promotion, not duplication.

Until this lands, the copied series is an archive with nothing appending to it.

## What would move

From `missingbulb/Sheepdog@main:.claudinite/local/packs/sheepdog-local/` (~2,500 lines total, no reference to the old repo name anywhere in it — it is portable verbatim):

**The task** — `tasks/fleet-digest/`: `task.md`, `task.mjs`, `worker.mjs`, `collect-fleet-day.mjs`, plus `collect-fleet-day.test.mjs` and `worker.test.mjs`. Prework enumerates active members, collects the previous UTC day's merged PRs and closed issues, drops the maintenance PRs that land in every member nightly, ranks by size of change and hands the agent a shortlist; on a day with nothing to rank the agent stage is skipped entirely and prework writes the brief itself. Backfill via `FORCE_TASKS=fleet-digest,DIGEST_BACKFILL_DAYS=N`, bounded at 30 days, skipping days that already have a brief.

**The checks it needs** — `digest-plain-text` (the brief is plain text despite its `.md` name; the notification renderer parses no markdown and collapses line breaks), `digest-config`, and `dated-fixture-collision`.

**Config** — a `digest` block on the `sheepdog` pack entry: `pick` (default 4) and `nudge` (on, 7 quiet days). Both default, so an existing sheepdog config keeps working untouched. Note the pack's existing "seeded config must agree exactly on both sides" rule applies if this ever reaches `packSeeds`.

**Secrets** — no new one. It reads `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`, adding only **Pull requests: read** on top of what the census already asks for.

Two of the pack's other local checks — `fleet-exclude-shape` and `managed-workflow-drift` — are worth a look in the same pass but are not part of the digest itself; `managed-workflow-drift` in particular may already be obsolete since the fleet-baseline workflow was retired (#749).

## Retention dependency

The only copy of this code is in `missingbulb/Sheepdog`. It should not be archived or deleted until this lands.

## Also worth a decision

`.claudinite/local/packs/sheepdog-local/RULES.md` (361 lines) carries the enforcer's accumulated lessons, and a good half of them are **not** enforcer-specific — the `ToolSearch` `mcp__github__` prefix rule, `Grep` needing `output_mode: "content"`, canon skills living under their pack rather than a flat `.claudinite/shared/skills/`, `ScheduleWakeup` needing a `prompt`, `verify-outcome.mjs` having no CLI, "ship the literal invocation rather than the file's name", and the `Claudinite tracker:` `in:title` + narrow `fields` lookup. Those are harness and Claudinite lessons that every member would benefit from, currently reachable only from a repo that is being retired. Worth routing through the growth lifecycle rather than losing with the repo — separable from this issue if preferred.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Shepherd/.claude/skills/merge-to-main

The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later, in the conversation half of the repo's scheduled `growth-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.
